Instrumental Music
in-struh-MEN-tul MYOO-zik
noun phrase
From Latin instrumentum (a tool, implement, means, from instruere, to furnish or arrange) and Latin musica (the art of music, from Greek mousike, art of the Muses). In Christian theology, the term designates the use of musical instruments in corporate worship — a practice present throughout the Old Testament Psalter (Ps. 150), employed in the temple under David's appointment (1 Chron. 23:5), debated among the Reformers under the Regulative Principle of Worship, and absent or present in Reformed churches according to their interpretation of that principle.

Biblical Definition

Instrumental music in worship refers to the use of musical instruments alongside or in support of congregational singing in the assembly of God's people. The Old Testament precedent is extensive and explicit. Psalm 150 commands praise with “trumpet sound,” “harp and lyre,” “timbrel,” “stringed instruments and pipe,” and “loud clashing cymbals.” David appointed four thousand Levites to praise the LORD with musical instruments (1 Chron. 23:5), and the temple orchestra was a formal feature of Israel's covenantal worship. In the book of Revelation, the twenty-four elders around the heavenly throne each hold a harp (Rev. 5:8), and the redeemed sing “as it were a new song before the throne” to harp accompaniment (Rev. 14:2–3).

The Reformation debate arose from the Regulative Principle: what Scripture does not command is not permitted in corporate worship. Calvin and the Reformed tradition noted that the instruments of the Levitical temple were part of the ceremonial order that has been fulfilled and set aside in Christ — as the Levitical priesthood was set aside, so too its instruments. The New Testament commands singing (Eph. 5:19; Col. 3:16) but does not explicitly command instruments. On this basis, the Reformed tradition historically divided: those who forbid instruments in corporate worship (exclusive psalmody congregations, many Scottish Presbyterians) and those who allow them as a circumstance of worship not regulated in kind. The question is not whether instruments are good — the Psalter commands them — but whether the ceremonial fulfillment in Christ removes the explicit mandate for their use in the new covenant assembly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defined instrument as “a tool; that by which work is performed; in music, any thing by which musical sounds are produced,” and music as “the art of combining sounds in a manner to please the ear.” The pairing designates music produced by physical instruments as distinct from voice alone.

expand to see more

INSTRUMENT, n. [L. instrumentum.] A tool; that by which work is performed or effect is produced. In music, any thing by which musical sounds are produced, whether by wind, string, or percussion.

MUSIC, n. [L. musica; Gr. mousike.] The art of combining sounds in a manner to please the ear. In its higher sense, music is the ordered and harmonious arrangement of sounds for the praise of God, the expression of human emotion, and the edification of the hearers.

Instrumental music in Scripture: the 150 Psalms contain numerous directives for musical instruments — harps, lyres, timbrels, trumpets, pipes, and cymbals — as part of the assembled worship of Israel. David appointed Levitical musicians as a permanent feature of the temple order.

In Reformation theology, the question of instrumental music in worship was decided by appeal to the Regulative Principle: whether the New Testament, which prescribes singing, also prescribes instruments, or whether the ceremonial temple order removed the express mandate for their use in the new covenant assembly.

The Scottish Covenanters, following Calvin's precedent in Geneva, removed organs from their churches on RPW grounds, while other Reformed bodies allowed instruments as circumstances of worship not regulated as to kind — a division that persists in the Reformed world today.

Key Scripture

Ps. 150:3 — "Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp."

1 Chron. 23:5 — "Moreover four thousand were porters; and four thousand praised the LORD with the instruments which I made, said David, to praise therewith."

Rev. 5:8 — "And when he had taken the book, the four beasts and four and twenty elders fell down before the Lamb, having every one of them harps, and golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints."

Ps. 33:2 — "Praise the LORD with harp: sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings."

Modern Corruption

Contemporary worship has inverted the proper use of instruments — turning them from servants of the sung Word into the primary vehicle of emotional manipulation, displacing the congregation's voice with professional performance.

expand to see more

The primary corruption of instrumental music in modern evangelical worship is its inversion from servant to master. In the biblical and Reformation pattern, instruments accompany the congregation's singing of God's Word; in the contemporary model, the “worship band” performs while the congregation watches and receives a musical experience. The electric guitar and drum kit, amplified to concert levels, create an emotional atmosphere that substitutes for the theological substance of sung Scripture. Where Calvin sought to make every worshiper an active singer of the Psalms, the contemporary worship industry has made every worshiper a passive audience member receiving a curated sound experience. This is not worship regulated by God's Word; it is entertainment marketed in religious vocabulary.

Within Reformed and Presbyterian churches, the Regulative Principle debate over instruments has at times produced a different corruption: a polemical austerity that suppresses the genuine Old Testament warrant for instrumental praise (Ps. 150; 1 Chron. 23:5) and reads the RPW in a manner so restrictive that even biblical patterns are excluded. The answer is not to resolve the debate by abandoning the RPW but to read it carefully: instruments that serve the congregation's singing of God's Word, at measured and intelligible volume, without displacing the human voice or manufactured emotional atmosphere, are difficult to condemn on the basis of the very Psalter that commands their use.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Latin root of instrument points to it as a tool — a means to an end, not an end in itself — and the history of Reformed worship has largely turned on whether instruments are kept in their proper servant role.

expand to see more

Latin instruere (to furnish, to equip, to build into) — the verb from which instrumentum derives; the sense is of a tool built for a specific purpose, not an ornament or end in itself

Latin instrumentum — a tool, implement, or means; entering English as instrument in the 14th century with its general sense preserved in theology, law, and music simultaneously

Greek organon (οργανον) — an instrument or tool; used in the Septuagint for the instruments of the Psalter; the root of organ, which became the church's dominant keyboard instrument in the medieval period

Hebrew keli-shir (כְלֵי שִיר) — instruments of song; the technical term in Chronicles (1 Chron. 15:16; 2 Chron. 5:13) for the Levitical temple instruments appointed by David

Old French instrument (12th c.) — tool, implement; entering Middle English via the French; the musical sense was dominant in religious and courtly contexts from the 13th century onward

Usage

"John Calvin removed the organ from Genevan worship not because he despised music but because he believed the Regulative Principle required warrant for every element of worship, and he found the New Testament's prescription to be the human voice singing Scripture — a principled decision that shaped Reformed worship for generations."

"The 1647 Westminster Directory for Public Worship, while not explicitly forbidding instruments, focused entirely on the congregation's sung Psalms — a context in which instruments, if used at all, were understood to serve the singing rather than to supplement or replace it."

"Isaac Watts, while advocating for hymns beyond the Psalter, still grounded his case in the Word and insisted that corporate song must edify the mind with scriptural truth, not merely stir the emotions — a principle that condemns both bare rationalism and experiential manipulation in equal measure."
